Where it began

Stuart Charles Glyndwr MacGill was born on 25 February 1971 in Mount Lawley, a suburb of Perth, and went to Christ Church Grammar School. Cricket ran in the family: his grandfather Charlie and his father Terry had each played for Western Australia before him.

He held a scholarship at the Australian Cricket Academy in 1990–1991 and made his own debut for Western Australia in 1993/94, but a single wicketless match was all he got. More than two years passed before he returned, this time for New South Wales, and took six wickets in his first game back. He also spent an English summer playing club cricket in Tiverton, in Devon.

The player

The 1997/98 season changed everything. He took 35 Sheffield Shield wickets and won his first Test cap at Adelaide, against South Africa, in January 1998. Later that year he was Australia's leading wicket-taker in Pakistan, and in the Ashes that followed he took 27 wickets at 17.70, including 7 for 50 and twelve in the match at Sydney.

His best figures came at Fatullah on Australia's first tour of Bangladesh, 8 for 108. He played 44 Tests from 1998 to 2008 and took 208 wickets at 29.03, with 12 five-wicket innings and two ten-wicket matches. Later, at 40, he turned out for the Sydney Sixers in the first Big Bash League and was part of the side that won the title at the WACA.

What made him special

He spun the ball hard and took wickets quickly. No modern leg-spinner was credited with a better strike rate, and when he reached 150 Test wickets it had taken him 8,312 balls, fewer than any spinner before him. At the Sydney Cricket Ground he took more five-wicket hauls than even Shane Warne, and both their names went up on the honours board there.

The one thing he lacked was luck with timing. He came along in the same years as Warne, so he was often the second spinner, or waiting for a chance. When the two bowled together in the West Indies, it was MacGill who did more of the damage, with 12 wickets in four Tests. As for his batting, a highest Test score of 43 suggests he was there mainly to keep the leg-spinners' union well represented.

Away from the middle

He was known as a man of wide interests. He earned a degree in viticulture and once got through 21 novels on a single tour of Pakistan. After his playing days he co-hosted SBS's coverage of the 2009 Ashes with Damien Martyn and Greg Matthews, and spent time as a breakfast radio host in Sydney.

And finally

In retirement he turned up as a guest on Plonk, a comedy series about wine. For a leg-spinner with a viticulture degree, it may be the most natural casting in television history.
